title: The Year 2000 Changed Men
author: Thinking West
summary: Thinking West argues that the shift from physical to sedentary, computer-based work beginning in the late 1980s and 1990s did more than change jobs; it began eroding male fitness and, the piece contends, masculinity itself, citing a roughly 1 percent annual decline in male testosterone since the 1980s linked to sedentary living. Tracing men's work from farming through factory labor to office and screen work, the author argues the modern gym exists precisely because digital life removed the physical demands that once kept men's bodies engaged, and previews a follow-on argument that screens' effects on men extend beyond the physical into the psyche.
points: Attributes measurable declines in male testosterone (roughly 1 percent per year since the 1980s) to the shift to sedentary, screen-based work and life.
Argues the computer, more than the office or the factory, made the male body 'economically irrelevant' for the first time in history.
Frames today's gym culture as an artificial replacement for physical labor men no longer perform by default.
Sets up a follow-on claim that screens' effects on men go beyond the physical into the psyche.
quotes: The most concerning measured result is the decline of testosterone among men at a rate of roughly 1% per year since the 1980s, suspected as a direct result of sedentary lifestyles.
Computational power far exceeded bodily power in terms of making or breaking a company. This had real effects on men.

Historically, being physically weak was somewhat marginalizing. In tribal societies, it made your participation in a hunt more difficult. But digital life removes that marginalization, allowing men's bodies to atrophy or grow overweight without immediate consequence.

One sign of our times is the gym; while in the past, the Greeks coined the term for the places they might spar or wrestle with one another, today's gym was effectively invented to recreate physical work. For most, it's a hobby we pursue voluntarily to ward off the effects of sedentary life.
Many of us know deep down that our ancestors were tougher men than us; the generations of WWI and WWII were a different breed. What's happened to men since then?
